title: Redis and Caching Architecture: TTLs, Invalidation, and Stampedes
learningObjectives: Explain why a cache helps and why it cannot replace the source of truth by default.
Trace a cache-aside read and write, including misses and stale values.
Choose TTL and invalidation behavior based on freshness requirements.
Explain cache stampedes, hot keys, and safe mitigation strategies.
Describe Redis memory, eviction, persistence, and replication trade-offs.
Design cache keys so tenant identity, authorization scope, and response-changing inputs cannot collide.

mentalModel.text: A cache is a faster, usually temporary copy of data that saves repeated work. It improves latency and reduces load when many requests reuse the same values, but it creates a second copy that can become stale. Design the miss path, update path, expiry policy, and failure behavior—not just the cache hit.

concepts.title: What a cache saves—and what it costs

blocks.text: A database query may need network time, query planning, disk access, joins, and row decoding. If many requests ask for the same result, a cache can avoid repeating some of that work.

blocks.title: Example request path
rows: Read a cached value and return it
a few to tens of milliseconds
Query the database and build the result
Read uncached pages or perform expensive work

blocks.title: These are examples, not guarantees
blocks.content: Actual latency depends on network distance, payload size, database plan, cache locality, load, and hardware. Measure p50/p95/p99 for your workload.

blocks.problem: A product detail page is requested 2,000 times per minute but the product changes only a few times per hour. Caching the product payload can avoid many repeated database reads.
reasoning: Cache the data that is expensive to recompute and likely to be reused.
Keep the database or another durable store as the source of truth unless the product explicitly accepts cache-only durability.
A cache adds memory cost, invalidation work, and another failure mode.
blocks.outcome: Use caching to reduce repeated work, not as a reflex for every query.

blocks.text: In cache-aside, the application checks the cache first. On a miss it reads the source of truth, puts the result in cache, and returns it. The application owns this logic.

blocks.title: Cache-aside read
Request sequence
rows: GET product:42 → hit on next request

blocks.title: Cache negative results carefully
blocks.content: If a product does not exist, repeated misses can hammer the database. A short negative-cache TTL can help, but be sure a newly created product becomes visible quickly enough.

blocks.problem: The first request misses and takes 12 ms to query the database. It caches the product. The next request hits the cache in 1 ms under this illustrative workload; the latency improvement disappears if the key expires or is evicted.
reasoning: A cache miss must have a correct fallback path.
Set a TTL or a deliberate invalidation rule so entries do not remain stale forever by accident.
Decide how database errors behave: do not turn a failed database read into a cached 'not found' response.
blocks.outcome: Cache-aside is simple and common, but cache misses, expiry, and source failures are part of the design.

concepts.title: Design cache keys without leaking data across tenants

blocks.text: A cache key identifies the result you are storing. If two requests can legitimately receive different responses, their cache entries must not accidentally share the same key. In a multi-tenant product, a product ID may only be unique inside one tenant, so a key such as `product:901` can collide across companies.

blocks.title: Example keys that include response identity
Which request details belong in the key?
rows: Include it if the representation changes
Include a stable scope/version if it changes the cached response, and still authorize the request

blocks.problem: Company A and Company B both have product ID 901. A cache key is built as `product:901`, and Company A's product contains private pricing.
reasoning: Company A's request fills `product:901` with its product details.
Company B requests its own product 901 but resolves to the same cache key, so the cache can return Company A's value.
Include tenant identity and every other input that changes the response in the key. Invalidate or version entries when that response context changes.
Keep normal authorization checks on every request; a well-designed key reduces accidental collisions but does not grant or deny access on its own.
blocks.outcome: A cache key is part of the data-isolation boundary. Build it from the identity and normalized inputs of the response, then enforce authorization independently.

blocks.title: Do not put secrets in cache keys
blocks.content: Use stable identifiers or versions for tenant and permission context, not raw access tokens or secret values. Cache-key separation prevents some collisions; it is not a substitute for authorization, tenant filtering, or safe invalidation.

blocks.text: A TTL limits how long an entry may remain in cache without refresh. It is a safety net, not a guarantee that data is always fresh. Invalidation removes or refreshes entries when the source changes.

blocks.title: Strategy
rows: Changes may remain stale until expiry
Write-through / update cache after DB write
Must handle partial failure between DB and cache
Delete cache key after DB commit
A race can refill stale data unless ordering is handled
More moving parts and operational failure modes

blocks.problem: A price is cached for 60 seconds. The database price changes one second after the cache entry is set. With TTL-only caching, readers may see the old price for roughly 59 more seconds.
reasoning: Choose freshness based on product rules: stale product descriptions may be acceptable; account balances or available inventory often need stronger controls.
If the database write succeeds but cache invalidation fails, stale data can remain. Record, retry, or otherwise design for that failure.
Cache invalidation after commit reduces one race but does not eliminate every concurrent refill race.
blocks.outcome: Pick a freshness target and document the maximum acceptable staleness and how invalidation failures recover.

concepts.title: Cache stampedes, hot keys, and overload

blocks.text: When a popular key expires, many requests may miss at once and all query the database. This is a cache stampede. A hot key can also overload one cache shard or become a single point of contention.

blocks.title: Common mitigations
blocks.content: Use per-key single-flight/request coalescing, a short lock where justified, TTL jitter, stale-while-revalidate, and bounded database concurrency. Each changes freshness or failure behavior, so pick based on the data.

blocks.problem: A product key expires while 800 requests per second arrive. Without coordination, a large fraction can all query the database before any request refills the cache.
reasoning: Single-flight lets one request refresh the value while others wait or use a permitted stale value.
TTL jitter spreads expirations so many keys do not all expire at the same instant.
A lock needs a timeout and safe release; never let a failed lock holder block refresh forever.
blocks.outcome: Protect the source of truth against synchronized misses, and measure miss rate, refresh concurrency, and database load.

concepts.title: Redis memory, eviction, persistence, and replication

blocks.text: Redis primarily serves data from memory, so capacity is a first-class limit. When memory reaches its configured limit, an eviction policy may remove keys. Redis persistence and replication can improve recovery or availability, but they do not automatically make every cache value durable or strongly consistent.

blocks.title: Concern
rows: Does not promise a key will remain cached
Can lose writes since the last snapshot
Durability depends on fsync policy and failure mode
Replica lag can expose stale reads; failover needs operational design

blocks.problem: If Redis is configured with a 4 GB maxmemory and a cache workload exceeds it, an eviction policy may remove keys to make room. The application must treat an evicted key as a cache miss and reload from the source.
reasoning: A cache should be safe to rebuild unless the system deliberately uses Redis as a durable data store.
Monitor memory, evictions, hit ratio, replication lag, persistence errors, and latency.
Persistence settings trade write latency and I/O for a smaller data-loss window; state the required recovery objective.
blocks.outcome: Plan for eviction, restarts, replica lag, and cache loss as normal operating conditions.

blocks.text: 1. Problem and motivation — A product endpoint repeatedly queries the database for the same product, but the cached price can become stale after an update.

2. Definition and design choice — Cache-aside checks Redis first, loads the source of truth on a miss, and stores the result with a TTL. The write path must define how stale entries are invalidated or refreshed.

blocks.problem: A product price is cached for 60 seconds. A price update commits to the database, but deleting the cache key fails.
reasoning: Until expiry or successful invalidation, readers may see the old price; TTL bounds the stale period only if the entry is not refreshed with stale data again.
Retry invalidation or publish a durable invalidation event after commit. Make consumers idempotent because events can be delivered more than once.
If the business cannot tolerate stale prices at checkout, revalidate against the source of truth at the decision point rather than trusting the cache.
blocks.outcome: A cache design is incomplete until it explains both hit behavior and the failure path when data changes.

blocks.text: 4. Trade-offs and scale — A high hit ratio can reduce database load, but large payloads, evictions, hot keys, and stampedes can erase the benefit. Measure hit ratio, miss latency, p95/p99, evictions, and source load.

5. Anti-patterns — Treating cached data as authoritative by accident, caching database errors as empty results, using one synchronized TTL for every key, and assuming Redis persistence eliminates every data-loss scenario.
6. Interview probes — What happens on a miss? How stale can the value become? What if invalidation fails? What if 800 requests miss the same key? What does the app do when Redis is unavailable?

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.title: A cache outage can become a database outage
tradeoffsAndPitfalls.content: If every request falls back to the database at full concurrency, a Redis outage can overwhelm the source. Use timeouts, bounded fallback concurrency, load shedding, and recovery plans.

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.title: Tenant-aware keys are necessary but not sufficient
tradeoffsAndPitfalls.content: Include tenant and response context in cache keys, but still enforce authorization and tenant scoping in the request path. Never rely on obscurity of a cache key to protect data.

revisionSheet.text: Cache-aside: cache read → on miss read source → cache value with TTL → return result.
TTL limits entry lifetime; invalidation tries to make changes visible sooner. Neither eliminates every race.
A stampede is many concurrent misses for the same key. Use single-flight, TTL jitter, stale-while-revalidate, or bounded refresh work.
Redis memory limits and eviction mean keys can disappear. Treat cache loss as a normal path.
Monitor hit ratio, miss rate, evictions, hot keys, latency, memory, source load, and replica lag.
Cache keys must distinguish tenants and every input that changes the response; a key is not an authorization check.

questions.prompt: In cache-aside, what normally happens on a cache miss?

options.text: Return the missing value as null without checking the source
Read the source of truth, cache the result if appropriate, then return it
Restart Redis

questions.explanation: The miss path reads the authoritative source and may populate the cache for later requests.
questions.hint: Think of the cache as a shortcut, not the source.

questions.prompt: Which data should generally remain the source of truth in a cache-aside design?

options.text: The durable database or authoritative store
Whichever copy was read most recently
The cache because it is faster

questions.explanation: The cache is a performance layer and can be evicted or lost.
questions.hint: Which copy can be rebuilt from the other?

questions.prompt: What can happen when Redis reaches maxmemory under an eviction policy?

options.text: The application can assume all keys remain forever
Keys may be evicted and must be reloadable if they are cache entries
The database stops accepting writes

questions.explanation: Memory limits and eviction mean a cache key can disappear at any time under pressure.

questions.prompt: The database update succeeds but deleting the cache key fails. What is the risk?

options.text: Readers may see stale cached data
The database automatically rolls back
All cache keys become valid

questions.explanation: The source changed but the cached copy remains until expiry or successful refresh/invalidation.

questions.prompt: Reading from a Redis replica always returns the latest write made to the primary.
questions.explanation: Replication can be asynchronous, so replica reads may lag behind the primary.

questions.prompt: A Redis cache should normally tolerate losing or evicting cache entries by reloading them from the authoritative source.
questions.explanation: A cache is generally a rebuildable performance layer; if Redis is the durable source of truth, that is a different architecture and needs explicit durability guarantees.

questions.prompt: Redis reaches maxmemory and evicts a cached product key. What should the application do?

options.text: Expect a cache miss and reload from the authoritative data source
Report the product as deleted
Assume replication guarantees the key is present everywhere forever
Disable database fallback

questions.explanation: Eviction is a normal cache operating condition; callers must tolerate misses and protect the source against refill surges.

questions.prompt: Redis is unavailable during a traffic spike. Which fallback is safest?

options.text: Let every request immediately open a new database connection with no bound
Use a bounded source fallback with timeouts, concurrency limits/backpressure, and a clear degraded response when saturated
Treat all cache misses as deleted data
Retry Redis forever in the request path

questions.explanation: A cache outage can turn into a database outage if every request bypasses cache without limits. Protect the source with deadlines, bounded concurrency, and load shedding when needed.

questions.prompt: Why might returning a short-lived stale value be safer than refreshing a hot key for every request?

options.text: It can reduce synchronized refresh work when the business permits bounded staleness
A stale value is always correct
It removes the need for a source of truth
It guarantees write atomicity across Redis and PostgreSQL

questions.explanation: Stale-while-revalidate is a business-dependent option: it lowers refresh pressure when bounded staleness is acceptable, but must not be used for data where stale decisions are unsafe.

questions.prompt: A value has a 60-second TTL. What does this tell you?

options.text: The value is always perfectly fresh
The entry is eligible to expire after its TTL, but stale reads can occur before then
The database value cannot change for 60 seconds

questions.explanation: TTL limits how long an entry lives; it does not guarantee immediate propagation of updates.
questions.hint: TTL is not the same as invalidation.

options.text: Many requests miss the same expired key and overload the source
A database backup
A Redis key that is always fresh

questions.explanation: Synchronized misses can trigger a burst of identical source queries.
questions.hint: Think about what happens when a popular key expires.

questions.prompt: Two tenants can both have product ID 901. A cache uses the key `product:901`. What is the main risk and appropriate fix?

options.text: No risk; Redis automatically checks tenant permissions
One tenant could receive the other tenant's cached value; include tenant and other response-changing context in the key and still authorize the request
The index will be slower
Use a longer TTL so data becomes tenant-specific

questions.explanation: A cache key must distinguish tenant-scoped values and any other input that changes the response. Key design reduces accidental cross-tenant collisions, but authorization must still be enforced independently.

interviewScenarios.prompt: A product price changes in the database, but users still see the old price from Redis. Explain the likely cause and design a robust update path.
strongAnswerPoints: Use durable retry/event delivery or a reconciliation path, with idempotent consumers.
Revalidate critical prices at checkout if stale data is unacceptable.
pitfalls: Assuming a successful database commit also updates Redis
Relying on TTL without stating the staleness budget
Treating cache values as authoritative for payment decisions
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: The database and Redis are separate systems, so the database write can succeed while cache invalidation fails. I would commit the database update, arrange reliable invalidation or an outbox event with retries, and use a TTL as a fallback bound. For checkout, I would validate the price against the authoritative store if stale prices could cause a financial error.

interviewScenarios.prompt: A popular key expires while hundreds of requests arrive per second. The database CPU spikes. How do you prevent a cache stampede?
strongAnswerPoints: Explain synchronized misses and duplicate source queries.
Use request coalescing/single-flight, TTL jitter, or stale-while-revalidate where acceptable.
Bound refresh concurrency and source fallback during cache outages.
Monitor miss rate, refresh concurrency, database load, and tail latency.
pitfalls: Increasing database connections without controlling concurrent misses
Using a lock with no timeout or safe release
Serving stale values without checking whether the product allows it
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: Many requests miss the same key before the first refill completes, so each may query the database. I would coalesce refreshes per key, add TTL jitter, and consider stale-while-revalidate if the freshness requirements allow it. I would also bound database fallback concurrency and monitor miss rate and p95/p99 latency.
